Statistical Optimal Transport

Optimal transport is rarely evaluated on population measures directly. In machine learning and statistics, the inputs are usually empirical laws, histograms, simulated particles or minibatches, and the central question is therefore no longer only how to compute OT, but how OT behaves as a random estimator. This chapter studies this statistical layer: qualitative consistency of empirical measures, non-asymptotic sample-complexity rates, and asymptotic bias--variance decompositions for exact and regularized transport costs.

This statistical convergence is conceptually different from the algorithmic convergence studied in the previous chapter. There the marginals and the temperature were fixed and one asked how Sinkhorn iterates approach a regularized optimizer. Here the number of samples grows, the empirical measures themselves move, and the regularization parameter may either remain fixed or be sent to zero. The resulting picture explains why exact OT is statistically expensive in high intrinsic dimension, why fixed-temperature Sinkhorn has smoother parametric fluctuations, and why approximating exact OT with entropy always involves a bias--variance tradeoff.

Law of Large Numbers and Central Limit Theorem¶

Before discussing sample complexity, it is useful to separate consistency from rates. If X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ are i.i.d. samples with common law α\alphaα, the associated empirical measure is the random probability measure

α^n:=1n∑i=1nδXi.\hat\alpha_n \eqdef \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}.α^n​:=n1​i=1∑n​δXi​​.
(1)

The ordinary law of large numbers says that empirical averages converge to expectations. In measure language this means that α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ converges weakly toward α\alphaα, because testing α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ against a bounded continuous function φ\varphiφ gives the sample average n−1∑iφ(Xi)n^{-1}\sum_i\varphi(X_i)n−1∑i​φ(Xi​). Wasserstein distances strengthen this statement by also recording moment convergence. Thus, if α\alphaα has a finite ppp-th moment, the empirical law converges to α\alphaα in Wp\Wass_pWp​, almost surely and in ppp-th mean in the sense that EWp(α^n,α)p→0\mathbb E\Wass_p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)^p\to0EWp​(α^n​,α)p→0. This is the qualitative consistency statement behind empirical OT plug-in estimators: empirical transport distances converge to their population counterparts once the sampled laws themselves converge in Wasserstein distance. It says nothing yet about the speed, which is the topic of Sample Complexity.

Central-Limit Fluctuations¶

The previous proposition is a law-of-large-numbers statement: a random empirical measure converges to the law that generated it. The central limit theorem describes a different, fluctuation-scale limit. As recalled in Remark Remark: Central limit theorem, if (Xi)i≥1(X_i)_{i\geq1}(Xi​)i≥1​ are centered i.i.d. random vectors with identity covariance, the law of n−1/2∑iXin^{-1/2}\sum_i X_in−1/2∑i​Xi​ converges weakly toward a Gaussian. Equivalently, if α\alphaα is the common law of the XiX_iXi​, this law is the rescaled convolution (D1/n)♯α∗n(D_{1/\sqrt n})_\sharp\alpha^{*n}(D1/n​​)♯​α∗n. Wasserstein distances make this qualitative convergence quantitative. The next result is a W1\Wass_1W1​ form of the Berry--Esseen theorem: it controls the error uniformly over all 1-Lipschitz test functions. The qualitative Bernoulli example was visualized earlier in Figure Div.

Empirical-Process Fluctuations¶

The fluctuation object used by statistical OT is the empirical law itself, not only a normalized sum in Euclidean space. There is no canonical Gaussian law on an unrestricted infinite-dimensional space of signed measures, so the precise finite-dimensional statement is made through test functions. Uniform convergence over an infinite class requires a Donsker condition Vaart & Wellner, 1996.

Proposition: Finite-Dimensional Empirical-Process CLT

Let X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\ldotsX1​,X2​,… be i.i.d. with law α\alphaα, and let φ1,…,φq∈L2(α)\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_q\in L^2(\alpha)φ1​,…,φq​∈L2(α). Then

n(∫φr d(α^n−α))r=1q⟹Gα,\sqrt n\left(\int\varphi_r\,d(\hat\alpha_n-\alpha)\right)_{r=1}^q \Longrightarrow G_\alpha,n​(∫φr​d(α^n​−α))r=1q​⟹Gα​,
(19)

where GαG_\alphaGα​ is centered Gaussian in Rq\RR^qRq with covariance

E[(Gα)r(Gα)s]=∫(φr−∫φr dα)(φs−∫φs dα)dα.\mathbb E[(G_\alpha)_r(G_\alpha)_s] = \int\left(\varphi_r-\int\varphi_r\,d\alpha\right) \left(\varphi_s-\int\varphi_s\,d\alpha\right)d\alpha.E[(Gα​)r​(Gα​)s​]=∫(φr​−∫φr​dα)(φs​−∫φs​dα)dα.
(20)
Proof

Apply the multivariate central limit theorem to the centered i.i.d. vectors (φr(Xi)−∫φr dα)r=1q(\varphi_r(X_i)-\int\varphi_r\,d\alpha)_{r=1}^q(φr​(Xi​)−∫φr​dα)r=1q​.

This linear CLT is the input to the delta-method arguments in Bias and Variance of OT. Exact OT may have only directional derivatives, whereas fixed-temperature entropic OT is smooth in the relative interiors of finite probability simplices.

Sample Complexity¶

This section compares four statistical regimes. Exact OT resolves geometry at all scales and pays rates controlled by the intrinsic dimension. MMD replaces transport by a kernel mean embedding and has a parametric Monte-Carlo rate for bounded kernels. Fixed-temperature Sinkhorn divergences smooth the dual potentials and also recover parametric fluctuations, at the price of regularization bias. Sliced Wasserstein inherits one-dimensional empirical rates through its projected laws.

Unregularized OT¶

The previous section proves qualitative convergence of empirical laws. The sample-complexity question is how fast this convergence happens. The sample complexity of unregularized OT suffers from the curse of dimensionality, but the relevant dimension is geometric. If the distributions are supported on a regular lower-dimensional set, for instance a d′d'd′-dimensional submanifold of Rd\RR^dRd, the empirical rate is governed by d′d'd′ rather than by the ambient dimension ddd. In the high-dimensional regime for Wp\Wass_pWp​, namely d′>2pd'>2pd′>2p, this gives the characteristic rate n−1/d′n^{-1/d'}n−1/d′. Exact OT is therefore dimension-adaptive: it sees the intrinsic dimension of the data support through its covering numbers Dudley, 1969Weed & Bach, 2019. Related two-sample-testing viewpoints are developed in Ramdas et al., 2017.

Figure Div gives a numerical overview: exact OT exhibits dimension-dependent empirical fluctuations, whereas MMD and fixed-temperature Sinkhorn divergences lie much closer to the parametric n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 scale.

Proof Sketch

Match the common mass inside the finest cells, then recursively match the remaining common mass inside each parent cell. Mass first matched at scale jjj moves by at most d,2−j\sqrt d,2^{-j}d​,2−j, and its total amount is bounded by the sum of the child-cell imbalances. The residual at the finest unresolved scale has mass at most one and moves by at most d,2−J\sqrt d,2^{-J}d​,2−J.

Let α\alphaα and β\betaβ be supported on [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d, and let α^n,β^m\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_mα^n​,β^​m​ be independent empirical measures. Then

E∣W1(α^n,β^m)−W1(α,β)∣≲drd(n)+rd(m),\mathbb E\left| \Wass_1(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) \right| \lesssim_d r_d(n)+r_d(m),E∣∣​W1​(α^n​,β^​m​)−W1​(α,β)∣∣​≲d​rd​(n)+rd​(m),

where

rd(N)={N−1/2,d=1,(log⁡N)N−1/2,d=2,N−1/d,d≥3.r_d(N)= \begin{cases} N^{-1/2}, & d=1,\\ (\log N)N^{-1/2}, & d=2,\\ N^{-1/d}, & d\geq3. \end{cases}rd​(N)=⎩⎨⎧​N−1/2,(logN)N−1/2,N−1/d,​d=1,d=2,d≥3.​

For Wp\Wass_pWp​ on a regular d′d'd′-dimensional support, the high-dimensional rate is N−1/d′N^{-1/d'}N−1/d′ when d′>2pd'>2pd′>2p under the usual volume-growth and moment assumptions. The dimension is therefore intrinsic rather than necessarily ambient.

The triangle inequality reduces the result to EW1(α^N,α)\mathbb E\Wass_1(\hat\alpha_N,\alpha)EW1​(α^N​,α). For each dyadic cell QQQ,

E∣α^N(Q)−α(Q)∣≤α(Q)/N.\mathbb E|\hat\alpha_N(Q)-\alpha(Q)| \leq \sqrt{\alpha(Q)/N}.E∣α^N​(Q)−α(Q)∣≤α(Q)/N​.

EW1(α^N,α)≲d2−J+N−1/2∑j=0J−12j(d/2−1).\mathbb E\Wass_1(\hat\alpha_N,\alpha) \lesssim_d 2^{-J}+N^{-1/2}\sum_{j=0}^{J-1}2^{j(d/2-1)}.EW1​(α^N​,α)≲d​2−J+N−1/2j=0∑J−1​2j(d/2−1).

Optimizing JJJ yields the three displayed regimes. Replacing dyadic cubes by covers of cardinality O(2jd′)O(2^{jd'})O(2jd′) gives the intrinsic-dimensional extension Dudley, 1969Fournier & Guillin, 2015Weed & Bach, 2019.

Lower Bounds and Minimax Optimality¶

The high-dimensional rate is not merely a defect of the empirical plug-in estimator. A hypercube of localized density perturbations gives the following distribution-estimation obstruction Singh & Póczos, 2018Weed & Bach, 2019Chewi et al., 2025.

Proposition: Minimax Lower Bound for Bounded Densities

Let d≥3d\geq3d≥3 and let A\mathcal AA contain the laws on [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d with density ρ\rhoρ satisfying 1/2≤ρ≤3/21/2\leq\rho\leq3/21/2≤ρ≤3/2. Then

inf⁡α~Nsup⁡α∈AEαW1(α~N,α)≥cdN−1/d,\inf_{\widetilde\alpha_N}\sup_{\alpha\in\mathcal A} \mathbb E_\alpha\Wass_1(\widetilde\alpha_N,\alpha) \geq c_dN^{-1/d},αN​inf​α∈Asup​Eα​W1​(αN​,α)≥cd​N−1/d,
(26)

where the infimum is over every estimator based on NNN i.i.d. samples.

Proof Sketch

Partition the cube into M=mdM=m^dM=md cells of width h=1/mh=1/mh=1/m, and put an independent signed, zero-mean bump of fixed small amplitude in each cell. Kantorovich--Rubinstein duality gives a separation of order hd+1h^{d+1}hd+1 per differing sign. Neighboring experiments have one-sample KL divergence O(hd)O(h^d)O(hd), so choosing M≍NM\asymp NM≍N keeps their NNN-sample total variation bounded away from one. Assouad’s lemma then gives Mhd+1=h≍N−1/dMh^{d+1}=h\asymp N^{-1/d}Mhd+1=h≍N−1/d.

Leveraging Smoothness¶

Smooth densities permit a better estimator: first remove fine empirical oscillations with a wavelet or kernel smoother, then compute OT between the smoothed laws Niles-Weed & Berthet, 2022.

Proposition: Smoothed Plug-In Rates

Let d≥3d\geq3d≥3, s>0s>0s>0, and suppose the source and target densities on [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d are bounded above and below and lie in a bounded B∞,∞sB^s_{\infty,\infty}B∞,∞s​ class. There are normalized nonnegative wavelet estimators α~n,β~m\tilde\alpha_n,\tilde\beta_mα~n​,β~​m​ such that

E∣W1(α~n,β~m)−W1(α,β)∣≤C(n−s+1d+2s+m−s+1d+2s).\mathbb E\left| \Wass_1(\tilde\alpha_n,\tilde\beta_m)-\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) \right| \leq C\left(n^{-\frac{s+1}{d+2s}}+m^{-\frac{s+1}{d+2s}}\right).E∣∣​W1​(α~n​,β~​m​)−W1​(α,β)∣∣​≤C(n−d+2ss+1​+m−d+2ss+1​).
(27)
Proof Sketch

At wavelet scale JJJ, the B1,1−1B^{-1}_{1,1}B1,1−1​ approximation bias is O(2−J(s+1))O(2^{-J(s+1)})O(2−J(s+1)) and the stochastic term is O(N−1/22J(d/2−1))O(N^{-1/2}2^{J(d/2-1)})O(N−1/22J(d/2−1)). Since W1\Wass_1W1​ is controlled by this negative Besov norm for densities bounded away from zero, balancing the two terms with 2J≍N1/(d+2s)2^J\asymp N^{1/(d+2s)}2J≍N1/(d+2s) gives the rate. Projection onto nonnegative unit-mass densities preserves its order.

This gain is statistical rather than automatically computational: a grid at bandwidth hhh has O(h−d)O(h^{-d})O(h−d) degrees of freedom, so direct smoothing remains expensive in high dimension. Sum-of-squares relaxations offer theoretical dimension-free exponents but are still costly in practice Vacher et al., 2021.

when k(x,x)≤κ2k(x,x)\leq\kappa^2k(x,x)≤κ2.

Entropic OT¶

Entropic regularization keeps the transport geometry while smoothing the dual potentials. The sharp fixed-temperature statement below has polynomial, rather than exponential, dependence on the inverse temperature Genevay et al., 2019Mena & Niles-Weed, 2019.

Proposition: Fixed-Temperature Sinkhorn Divergence Has a Parametric Rate

Let c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2/2c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2, and assume α\alphaα and β\betaβ are σ2\sigma^2σ2-subgaussian on Rd\RR^dRd:

∫e∥x∥2/(2dσ2)dα(x)≤2,∫e∥y∥2/(2dσ2)dβ(y)≤2.\int e^{\norm{x}^2/(2d\sigma^2)}d\alpha(x)\leq2, \qquad \int e^{\norm{y}^2/(2d\sigma^2)}d\beta(y)\leq2.∫e∥x∥2/(2dσ2)dα(x)≤2,∫e∥y∥2/(2dσ2)dβ(y)≤2.
(32)

Set

qd=⌈5d2⌉+6,bd=⌈5d4⌉+3,Λd,σ(ϵ)=ϵ(1+σqdϵbd).q_d=\left\lceil\frac{5d}{2}\right\rceil+6, \qquad b_d=\left\lceil\frac{5d}{4}\right\rceil+3, \qquad \Lambda_{d,\sigma}(\epsilon) =\epsilon\left(1+\frac{\sigma^{q_d}}{\epsilon^{b_d}}\right).qd​=⌈25d​⌉+6,bd​=⌈45d​⌉+3,Λd,σ​(ϵ)=ϵ(1+ϵbd​σqd​​).
(33)

For independent empirical measures and every ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0,

E∣Lˉcϵ(α^n,β^m)−Lˉcϵ(α,β)∣≤CdΛd,σ(ϵ)(1n+1m).\mathbb E\left| \bar\MK_c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) -\bar\MK_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta) \right| \leq C_d\Lambda_{d,\sigma}(\epsilon) \left(\frac1{\sqrt n}+\frac1{\sqrt m}\right).E∣∣​Lˉcϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Lˉcϵ​(α,β)∣∣​≤Cd​Λd,σ​(ϵ)(n​1​+m​1​).
(34)

Thus fixed temperature gives a parametric rate, while the prefactor grows only polynomially as ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow0ϵ↓0.

Proof Sketch

Dual optimality bounds a one-marginal perturbation by the empirical process indexed by normalized entropic potentials. Mena--Niles-Weed prove polynomial local Hölder bounds for these potentials under a common subgaussian proxy. Their covering numbers have a finite Dudley integral, hence the empirical process is O(n−1/2)O(n^{-1/2})O(n−1/2) with constant Cd(1+σqd)C_d(1+\sigma^{q_d})Cd​(1+σqd​) at ϵ=1\epsilon=1ϵ=1. The rescaling x↦x/ϵx\mapsto x/\sqrt\epsilonx↦x/ϵ​ gives the displayed Λd,σ(ϵ)\Lambda_{d,\sigma}(\epsilon)Λd,σ​(ϵ). Perturbing both marginals and applying the same estimate to the cross and two self terms yields the debiased result.

Sample Complexity of Estimating OT Maps¶

The preceding estimates concern transport values. For map estimation, one solves the empirical dual problem for potentials (fn,mϵ,gn,mϵ)∈Rn×Rm(\mathbf f_{n,m}^\epsilon,\mathbf g_{n,m}^\epsilon)\in\RR^n\times\RR^m(fn,mϵ​,gn,mϵ​)∈Rn×Rm, with ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0 denoting the unregularized Kantorovich problem, and then uses the soft ccc-transform as an out-of-sample extrapolator.

For the quadratic cost c2(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2c_2(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^2/2c2​(x,y)=∥x−y∥2/2, let Pn,mϵ=(Pijϵ)\P_{n,m}^\epsilon=(\P_{ij}^\epsilon)Pn,mϵ​=(Pijϵ​) be the empirical entropic coupling and let gn,mϵ\mathbf g_{n,m}^\epsilongn,mϵ​ be the target-side dual potential. Define

un,mϵ(x)=−ϵlog⁡∑jbjexp⁡(gn,m,jϵ−c2(x,Yj)ϵ),Tn,mϵ(x)=x−∇un,mϵ(x).u_{n,m}^\epsilon(x) = -\epsilon\log \sum_j b_j \exp\left( \frac{\mathbf g_{n,m,j}^\epsilon-c_2(x,Y_j)}{\epsilon} \right), \qquad T_{n,m}^\epsilon(x)=x-\nabla u_{n,m}^\epsilon(x).un,mϵ​(x)=−ϵlogj∑​bj​exp(ϵgn,m,jϵ​−c2​(x,Yj​)​),Tn,mϵ​(x)=x−∇un,mϵ​(x).
(35)

Equivalently, subtracting the quadratic marginal terms turns c2c_2c2​ into the bilinear cost cip(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩c_{\rm ip}(x,y)=-\langle x,y\ranglecip​(x,y)=−⟨x,y⟩. With the sign convention used here, the associated soft convex potential is

φn,mϵ(x)=12∥x∥2−un,mϵ(x)=ϵlog⁡∑jbjexp⁡(⟨x,Yj⟩+gn,m,jϵ−12∥Yj∥2ϵ),Tn,mϵ=∇φn,mϵ.\varphi_{n,m}^\epsilon(x) = \frac12\norm{x}^2-u_{n,m}^\epsilon(x) = \epsilon\log\sum_j b_j \exp\left( \frac{\langle x,Y_j\rangle+\mathbf g_{n,m,j}^\epsilon-\frac12\norm{Y_j}^2}{\epsilon} \right), \qquad T_{n,m}^\epsilon=\nabla\varphi_{n,m}^\epsilon .φn,mϵ​(x)=21​∥x∥2−un,mϵ​(x)=ϵlogj∑​bj​exp(ϵ⟨x,Yj​⟩+gn,m,jϵ​−21​∥Yj​∥2​),Tn,mϵ​=∇φn,mϵ​.
(36)

Differentiating this log-sum-exp gives the explicit soft barycentric form

Tn,mϵ(x)=∑jωjϵ(x)Yj,ωjϵ(x)=bje(gn,m,jϵ−c2(x,Yj))/ϵ∑kbke(gn,m,kϵ−c2(x,Yk))/ϵ.T_{n,m}^\epsilon(x)=\sum_j\omega_j^\epsilon(x)Y_j, \qquad \omega_j^\epsilon(x)= \frac{b_j e^{(\mathbf g_{n,m,j}^\epsilon-c_2(x,Y_j))/\epsilon}} {\sum_k b_k e^{(\mathbf g_{n,m,k}^\epsilon-c_2(x,Y_k))/\epsilon}} .Tn,mϵ​(x)=j∑​ωjϵ​(x)Yj​,ωjϵ​(x)=∑k​bk​e(gn,m,kϵ​−c2​(x,Yk​))/ϵbj​e(gn,m,jϵ​−c2​(x,Yj​))/ϵ​.
(37)

At a sampled point XiX_iXi​, Sinkhorn normalization gives

Tn,mϵ(Xi)=1ai∑jPijϵYj,T_{n,m}^\epsilon(X_i)=\frac1{a_i}\sum_jP_{ij}^\epsilon Y_j,Tn,mϵ​(Xi​)=ai​1​j∑​Pijϵ​Yj​,
(38)

which is the barycentric projection of the entropic plan. At ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0, the hard ccc-transform is generally nondifferentiable: away from Laguerre boundaries its gradient selects one target site, whereas the barycentric projection of an optimal unregularized plan may average several target sites when a row splits. The consistency statement is therefore formulated directly for barycentric projections. It uses uniform empirical weights; deterministic nonuniform weights require the corresponding entropy bound.

Proposition: Consistency of Empirical Barycentric Maps

Let Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset\RR^dΩ⊂Rd be compact, let α,β∈P2(Ω)\alpha,\beta\in\Pp_2(\Omega)α,β∈P2​(Ω), and assume that α\alphaα is absolutely continuous. Let ϕ\phiϕ be a Brenier potential and choose a bounded Borel subgradient selection T(x)∈∂ϕ(x)T(x)\in\partial\phi(x)T(x)∈∂ϕ(x), which equals the unique Brenier map at every differentiability point. If uniform empirical measures α^n,β^m\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_mα^n​,β^​m​ converge to α,β\alpha,\betaα,β in W2\Wass_2W2​, if ϵn,m→0\epsilon_{n,m}\to0ϵn,m​→0 with ϵn,mlog⁡(min⁡{n,m})→0\epsilon_{n,m}\log(\min\{n,m\})\to0ϵn,m​log(min{n,m})→0, and if Tˉn,mϵ\bar T_{n,m}^{\epsilon}Tˉn,mϵ​ is the barycentric projection of the empirical entropic coupling, then

∫∥Tˉn,mϵ(x)−T(x)∥2 dα^n(x)⟶0.\int\norm{\bar T_{n,m}^{\epsilon}(x)-T(x)}^2\,d\hat\alpha_n(x) \longrightarrow0.∫∥∥​Tˉn,mϵ​(x)−T(x)∥∥​2dα^n​(x)⟶0.
(39)

The analogous backward statement holds when β\betaβ is also absolutely continuous.

Proof Sketch

Compare the entropic minimizer with an unregularized empirical optimal plan. On a uniform n×mn\times mn×m grid, this relative entropy is the mutual information of two uniform indices and is at most min⁡{log⁡n,log⁡m}\min\{\log n,\log m\}min{logn,logm}. Thus the entropic coupling has asymptotically optimal quadratic cost when ϵlog⁡(min⁡{n,m})→0\epsilon\log(\min\{n,m\})\to0ϵlog(min{n,m})→0. Any weak limit is therefore an optimal population plan, hence the Brenier graph (Id⁡,T)#α(\operatorname{Id},T)_\#\alpha(Id,T)#​α. Jensen’s inequality applied to each conditional law reduces the claim to the convergence of ∬∥y−T(x)∥2 dPn,mϵ(x,y)\iint\norm{y-T(x)}^2\,dP_{n,m}^{\epsilon}(x,y)∬∥y−T(x)∥2dPn,mϵ​(x,y). This last convergence is not a continuity tautology, because the Brenier map is only defined α\alphaα-a.e. At every differentiability point of ϕ\phiϕ, the subdifferential is the singleton {∇ϕ(x)}\{\nabla\phi(x)\}{∇ϕ(x)}; compactness of the target bounds the selected subgradients, and the closed-graph property of the subdifferential then gives continuity of any selected subgradient there. Since convex functions are differentiable Lebesgue-a.e. and α\alphaα is absolutely continuous, the portmanteau theorem for bounded test functions continuous almost everywhere under the limiting measure gives the desired limit.

Quantitative map rates require stronger stability assumptions on Brenier potentials. For unregularized map estimation, Hütter--Rigollet, Deb--Ghosal--Sen, and Manole--Balakrishnan--Niles-Weed--Wasserman obtain, under smoothness and curvature assumptions, squared L2(α)L^2(\alpha)L2(α) risk of order

E∥T^n−T0∥L2(α)2≲(n−2s2(s−1)+d∨n−1)\mathbb E\norm{\widehat T_n-T_0}_{L^2(\alpha)}^2 \lesssim \left(n^{-\frac{2s}{2(s-1)+d}}\vee n^{-1}\right)E∥∥​Tn​−T0​∥∥​L2(α)2​≲(n−2(s−1)+d2s​∨n−1)
(40)

up to logarithms, and this rate is minimax optimal Hütter & Rigollet, 2021Deb et al., 2021Manole et al., 2024. For the Sinkhorn-computable entropic barycentric estimator, Pooladian--Niles-Weed prove

E∥Tϵ,(n,n)−T0∥L2(α)2≲ϵ−d/2log⁡(n)n−1/2+ϵ(sˉ+1)/2+ϵ2I0(α,β),\mathbb E\norm{T_{\epsilon,(n,n)}-T_0}_{L^2(\alpha)}^2 \lesssim \epsilon^{-d/2}\log(n)n^{-1/2} + \epsilon^{(\bar s+1)/2} + \epsilon^2\mathcal I_0(\alpha,\beta),E∥∥​Tϵ,(n,n)​−T0​∥∥​L2(α)2​≲ϵ−d/2log(n)n−1/2+ϵ(sˉ+1)/2+ϵ2I0​(α,β),
(41)

with sˉ=s∧3\bar s=s\wedge3sˉ=s∧3 Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021. The first term is the statistical fluctuation of the entropic map, while the last two terms are regularization-bias terms. Thus fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ gives a parametric empirical fluctuation for the regularized map, whereas ϵ≃n−1/(d+sˉ+1)\epsilon\simeq n^{-1/(d+\bar s+1)}ϵ≃n−1/(d+sˉ+1) gives a convergent estimator of the Brenier map. The unregularized case can achieve sharper minimax rates when combined with enough smooth extension machinery; the regularized estimator is instead directly Sinkhorn-computable.

Remark: No free lunch when approximating exact OT

The parametric rate in Proposition Proposition: Fixed-Temperature Sinkhorn Divergence Has a Parametric Rate holds for fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ. If the goal is to approximate the unregularized OT value, one must also account for the regularization bias. In a typical bounded-cost finite-dimensional regime,

∣Lˉcϵ(α,β)−Lc(α,β)∣≤Cϵ,E∣Lˉcϵ(α^n,β^n)−Lˉcϵ(α,β)∣≤Cd,σϵ−pdn−1/2,pd:=⌈5d4⌉+2,\abs{\bar\MK_\c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-\MK_\c(\alpha,\beta)} \leq C\epsilon, \qquad \EE\abs{\bar\MK_\c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_n)-\bar\MK_\c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)} \leq C_{d,\sigma}\epsilon^{-p_d}n^{-1/2}, \qquad p_d\eqdef\left\lceil\frac{5d}{4}\right\rceil+2,∣∣​Lˉcϵ​(α,β)−Lc​(α,β)∣∣​≤Cϵ,E∣∣​Lˉcϵ​(α^n​,β^​n​)−Lˉcϵ​(α,β)∣∣​≤Cd,σ​ϵ−pd​n−1/2,pd​:=⌈45d​⌉+2,
(42)

where the second estimate is the small-ϵ\epsilonϵ form of the polynomial Mena--Niles-Weed bound. Balancing the two terms gives ϵ≃n−1/(2(pd+1))\epsilon\simeq n^{-1/(2(p_d+1))}ϵ≃n−1/(2(pd​+1)) and total error of order n−1/(2(pd+1))n^{-1/(2(p_d+1))}n−1/(2(pd​+1)) under this conservative bound. Thus entropic smoothing improves the statistical behavior at fixed scale, and the refined analysis avoids an exponential eC/ϵe^{C/\epsilon}eC/ϵ penalty, but approximating exact OT still forces a bias-variance tradeoff whose exponent deteriorates with dimension.

The interactive demo below is only a scaling guide: change the dimension to see the exact-OT exponent flatten, and change ϵ\epsilonϵ to move the Sinkhorn bias floor against its parametric fluctuation term.

Sliced Wasserstein¶

For Pθ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩P_\theta(x)=\langle\theta,x\ranglePθ​(x)=⟨θ,x⟩ and normalized surface measure σ\sigmaσ on Sd−1\mathbb S^{d-1}Sd−1, define

SW⁡p(α,β)p=∫Sd−1Wp((Pθ)#α,(Pθ)#β)p,dσ(θ).\SW_p(\alpha,\beta)^p = \int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}} \Wass_p((P_\theta)_\#\alpha,(P_\theta)_\#\beta)^p,d\sigma(\theta).SWp​(α,β)p=∫Sd−1​Wp​((Pθ​)#​α,(Pθ​)#​β)p,dσ(θ).
(43)

The construction is studied in Sliced Wasserstein Distances. Statistically, it inherits one-dimensional empirical rates rather than ambient-dimensional matching rates Nadjahi et al., 2019Nadjahi et al., 2020Manole et al., 2022.

Theorem: Dimension-Free Empirical Rate for Sliced Wasserstein

Let p≥1p\geq1p≥1. Assume all one-dimensional projections satisfy

sup⁡θEWp((Pθ)#α^n,(Pθ)#α)p≤Aαn−p/2,sup⁡θEWp((Pθ)#β^m,(Pθ)#β)p≤Aβm−p/2.\sup_\theta\mathbb E\Wass_p((P_\theta)_\#\hat\alpha_n,(P_\theta)_\#\alpha)^p \leq A_\alpha n^{-p/2}, \qquad \sup_\theta\mathbb E\Wass_p((P_\theta)_\#\hat\beta_m,(P_\theta)_\#\beta)^p \leq A_\beta m^{-p/2}.θsup​EWp​((Pθ​)#​α^n​,(Pθ​)#​α)p≤Aα​n−p/2,θsup​EWp​((Pθ​)#​β^​m​,(Pθ​)#​β)p≤Aβ​m−p/2.

Then

E∣SW⁡p(α^n,β^m)−SW⁡p(α,β)∣≤Aα1/pn−1/2+Aβ1/pm−1/2.\mathbb E|\SW_p(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\SW_p(\alpha,\beta)| \leq A_\alpha^{1/p}n^{-1/2}+A_\beta^{1/p}m^{-1/2}.E∣SWp​(α^n​,β^​m​)−SWp​(α,β)∣≤Aα1/p​n−1/2+Aβ1/p​m−1/2.
(45)

For p=1p=1p=1, bounded support implies the assumption. For p=2p=2p=2, a sufficient condition is the uniform projected Bobkov--Ledoux J2J_2J2​ bound

sup⁡θ∫01[u(1−u)hα,θ(Qα,θ(u))2+u(1−u)hβ,θ(Qβ,θ(u))2] du<∞.\sup_\theta\int_0^1 \left[ \frac{u(1-u)}{h_{\alpha,\theta}(Q_{\alpha,\theta}(u))^2} +\frac{u(1-u)}{h_{\beta,\theta}(Q_{\beta,\theta}(u))^2} \right]\,du<\infty.θsup​∫01​[hα,θ​(Qα,θ​(u))2u(1−u)​+hβ,θ​(Qβ,θ​(u))2u(1−u)​]du<∞.
(46)
Proof

The triangle inequality reduces the claim to two one-sample sliced distances. Jensen’s inequality moves expectation inside the spherical integral, after which the assumed projected bounds apply. For p=1p=1p=1, use the Dvoretzky--Kiefer--Wolfowitz inequality and W1=∫∣Fα^n−Fα∣\Wass_1=\int|F_{\hat\alpha_n}-F_\alpha|W1​=∫∣Fα^n​​−Fα​∣. For p=2p=2p=2, use the one-dimensional J2J_2J2​ quantile-process estimate Bobkov & Ledoux, 2019.

Remark: Directions are another sample budget

The theorem concerns the statistical samples used to form α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ and β^m\hat\beta_mβ^​m​. In computation one also replaces the spherical average in the definition of SW⁡p\SW_pSWp​ by an empirical average over LLL random directions. For bounded support, the resulting Monte-Carlo error for SW⁡pp\SW_p^pSWpp​ is of order L−1/2L^{-1/2}L−1/2, independently of ddd, because it is just the average of bounded one-dimensional costs. This should not be read as saying that a small number of directions captures full W2\Wass_2W2​ geometry in high dimension. Even the exact sliced distance is an averaged projected geometry, not a bi-Lipschitz surrogate for W2\Wass_2W2​ uniformly in dimension; see Proposition Proposition: Metric Properties of Sliced Wasserstein and Intrinsic Sliced Length. Moreover, if a discrepancy is visible only inside a spherical cap of angular radius δ\deltaδ, the probability that LLL random directions hit it is roughly 1−(1−σ(capδ))L1-(1-\sigma(\mathrm{cap}_\delta))^L1−(1−σ(capδ​))L, and σ(capδ)\sigma(\mathrm{cap}_\delta)σ(capδ​) scales like δd−1\delta^{d-1}δd−1 for small caps. For a fixed narrow aperture, it decays exponentially with ddd. Thus estimating the sliced objective is dimension-friendly, while using random slices to approximate a worst direction, a max-sliced distance, or a proxy meant to behave like full W2\Wass_2W2​, reintroduces an angular-covering cost. This is the practical no-free-lunch behind sliced, max-sliced and subspace-sliced variants; see also Section Sliced Wasserstein Distances.

Bias and Variance of OT¶

The previous section answered a coarse but essential question: how many samples are needed before an empirical OT quantity is accurate, typically up to universal constants. We now ask for a finer statistical description. Rather than only estimating the size of the error, we seek the first expansion of the plug-in estimator. Given empirical laws α^n\hat\alpha_nα^n​ and β^m\hat\beta_mβ^​m​, and a scalar OT value V\mathcal VV, this expansion separates the leading statistical bias

Bn,m(V):=EV(α^n,β^m)−V(α,β)B_{n,m}(\mathcal V) \eqdef \mathbb E\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\mathcal V(\alpha,\beta)Bn,m​(V):=EV(α^n​,β^​m​)−V(α,β)
(47)

and the centered fluctuation

Zn,m(V):=V(α^n,β^m)−EV(α^n,β^m),Z_{n,m}(\mathcal V) \eqdef \mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) -\mathbb E\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m),Zn,m​(V):=V(α^n​,β^​m​)−EV(α^n​,β^​m​),
(48)

for values such as V(α,β)=Wpp(α,β)\mathcal V(\alpha,\beta)=\Wass_p^p(\alpha,\beta)V(α,β)=Wpp​(α,β), V(α,β)=Lc(α,β)\mathcal V(\alpha,\beta)=\MK_c(\alpha,\beta)V(α,β)=Lc​(α,β), or their entropic analogues. This goes beyond Proposition Proposition: Finite-Dimensional Empirical-Process CLT: the empirical fluctuation is now pushed through a nonlinear, often nonsmooth, transport value. The resulting law is governed by local differentiability and by the geometry of the optimal dual face.

Literature Map¶

The shape of the limit depends sharply on the analytic regularity of the transport value. For exact OT on a finite or countable space, the map from empirical weights to optimal cost is convex and piecewise affine. Sommerfeld and Munk Sommerfeld & Munk, 2018, and the countable-space extensions of Tameling--Sommerfeld--Munk Tameling et al., 2019, show that the natural limit is a directional delta-method limit: often a support function of a Gaussian process over an optimal dual face, rather than a Gaussian random variable. For Euclidean costs, del Barrio--Loubes and collaborators obtain central-limit theorems for empirical transportation costs under regularity and uniqueness assumptions on the Kantorovich potentials Barrio & Loubes, 2019Barrio et al., 2021. Entropic regularization makes the problem smoother. For fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, the value is differentiable with respect to the marginals, and the limiting variance is read directly from the entropic dual potentials. This is the point of view developed by Bigot--Cazelles--Papadakis, Klatt--Tameling--Munk, Hundrieser--Klatt--Munk, and Mena--Niles-Weed Bigot et al., 2019Klatt et al., 2020Hundrieser et al., 2021Mena & Niles-Weed, 2019. More recent results clarify weak limits beyond smooth costs and second-order null limits for Sinkhorn divergences González-Sanz & Hundrieser, 2023Goldfeld et al., 2024. These asymptotic statements do not replace the dimension-dependent bounds of Sample Complexity; they explain what the leading random object is, what constants appear, and where the bias comes from.

Bias Versus Centered Fluctuation¶

The decomposition

V(α^n,β^m)−V(α,β)=EV(α^n,β^m)−V(α,β)⏟bias+V(α^n,β^m)−EV(α^n,β^m)⏟centered fluctuation\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\mathcal V(\alpha,\beta) = \underbrace{\mathbb E\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\mathcal V(\alpha,\beta)}_{\text{bias}} + \underbrace{\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\mathbb E\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)}_{\text{centered fluctuation}}V(α^n​,β^​m​)−V(α,β)=biasEV(α^n​,β^​m​)−V(α,β)​​+centered fluctuationV(α^n​,β^​m​)−EV(α^n​,β^​m​)​​
(49)

is elementary, but in OT it is genuinely diagnostic because the two terms may live on different scales. For the self-distance V(α^n,α)=Wpp(α^n,α)\mathcal V(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)=\Wass_p^p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)V(α^n​,α)=Wpp​(α^n​,α), the population value is zero and the deterministic bias EWpp(α^n,α)\mathbb E\Wass_p^p(\hat\alpha_n,\alpha)EWpp​(α^n​,α) is the leading term. On a regular d′d'd′-dimensional support, the high-dimensional matching scale is n−p/d′n^{-p/d'}n−p/d′ when d′>2pd'>2pd′>2p, with a critical logarithmic correction when d′=2pd'=2pd′=2p. Below this threshold the rate is controlled by empirical-process fluctuations and can be faster; in one dimension, smooth positive densities give the familiar quantile-process asymptotics for Wpp\Wass_p^pWpp​, of order n−p/2n^{-p/2}n−p/2 for p>1p>1p>1, and in particular n−1n^{-1}n−1 for W22\Wass_2^2W22​. Thus p/d′p/d'p/d′ is the high-dimensional matching exponent, not a universal rate formula Dudley, 1969Fournier & Guillin, 2015Weed & Bach, 2019. By contrast, when V(α,β)\mathcal V(\alpha,\beta)V(α,β) is nonzero and the OT value is differentiable at (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β), the centered fluctuation is often governed by an ordinary n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2 central limit theorem. A ``slow OT statistic’’ can therefore have three distinct causes: a large empirical bias, a nonsmooth directional limit, or a regularization bias Lcϵ(α,β)−Lc(α,β)\MK_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-\MK_c(\alpha,\beta)Lcϵ​(α,β)−Lc​(α,β) that still has to be removed.

The multinomial central limit theorem gives

which is the finite-dimensional form of Danskin’s theorem already used in Proposition: First variations of unregularized OT. The directional delta method gives the displayed distributional limit. The same argument gives the independent two-sample limit. If N/(N+M)→λ∈(0,1)N/(N+M)\to\lambda\in(0,1)N/(N+M)→λ∈(0,1), then, with rN,M=NM/(N+M)r_{N,M}=\sqrt{NM/(N+M)}rN,M​=NM/(N+M)​,

where GaG_aGa​ and GbG_bGb​ are independent multinomial Gaussian limits. When both dual potentials are unique, the first-order bias is negligible and the asymptotic variance of the unscaled estimator is

1N∑iai(fi⋆−fˉ⋆)2+1M∑jbj(gj⋆−gˉ⋆)2,fˉ⋆=∑iaifi⋆,gˉ⋆=∑jbjgj⋆.\frac{1}{N}\sum_i a_i(f^\star_i-\bar f^\star)^2 + \frac{1}{M}\sum_j b_j(g^\star_j-\bar g^\star)^2, \qquad \bar f^\star=\sum_i a_i f_i^\star, \quad \bar g^\star=\sum_j b_j g_j^\star.N1​i∑​ai​(fi⋆​−fˉ​⋆)2+M1​j∑​bj​(gj⋆​−gˉ​⋆)2,fˉ​⋆=i∑​ai​fi⋆​,gˉ​⋆=j∑​bj​gj⋆​.

If the optimal face contains several dual potentials, the limit is the supremum of a Gaussian process over that face and need not itself be Gaussian. The leading bias is then the expectation of this supremum divided by the square-root sample size. This nonsmoothness is the basic reason why inference for exact OT can remain delicate even on a finite space.

This is a useful warning: the asymptotic law is determined not only by a rate, but also by the local geometry of the functional.

Three Error Terms When Entropy Estimates Exact OT¶

If the target is Lc(α,β)\MK_c(\alpha,\beta)Lc​(α,β) but the statistic uses Lcϵ\MK_c^\epsilonLcϵ​, three errors should be kept separate:

Lcϵ(α^n,β^m)−Lc(α,β)=Lcϵ(α,β)−Lc(α,β)⏟regularization bias+ELcϵ(α^n,β^m)−Lcϵ(α,β)⏟statistical bias+Lcϵ(α^n,β^m)−ELcϵ(α^n,β^m)⏟centered fluctuation.\MK_c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\MK_c(\alpha,\beta) = \underbrace{\MK_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-\MK_c(\alpha,\beta)}_{\text{regularization bias}} + \underbrace{\mathbb E\MK_c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)-\MK_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)}_{\text{statistical bias}} + \underbrace{\MK_c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m) -\mathbb E\MK_c^\epsilon(\hat\alpha_n,\hat\beta_m)}_{\text{centered fluctuation}} .Lcϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Lc​(α,β)=regularization biasLcϵ​(α,β)−Lc​(α,β)​​+statistical biasELcϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−Lcϵ​(α,β)​​+centered fluctuationLcϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)−ELcϵ​(α^n​,β^​m​)​​.
(68)

Although algebraic, this identity is important statistically. It is usually read after choosing ϵ=ϵn\epsilon=\epsilon_nϵ=ϵn​. For fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ, the statistical bias is typically O(n−1+m−1)O(n^{-1}+m^{-1})O(n−1+m−1) in finite dimension, and the centered fluctuation is OP(n−1/2+m−1/2)O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2})OP​(n−1/2+m−1/2); boundary events where an empirical finite histogram has a zero entry have exponentially small probability when the population weights are positive. The regularization bias disappears only when ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0, whereas the variance constants usually deteriorate as ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow0ϵ↓0. This is the asymptotic form of the bias--variance tradeoff illustrated in Div.

What Changes in Continuous Spaces¶

The finite-dimensional formulas above are not merely toy models; they are the cleanest template for the general mechanism. Whenever an OT value is Hadamard differentiable and admits a unique sufficiently regular dual potential f⋆f^\starf⋆, the empirical-process CLT and the delta method give a first-order Gaussian limit with one-sample variance Var⁡α(f⋆(X))\operatorname{Var}_\alpha(f^\star(X))Varα​(f⋆(X)). When differentiability fails, as can happen for exact OT because the dual optimizer is not unique or because one studies the degenerate self-distance Lc(α,α)=0\MK_c(\alpha,\alpha)=0Lc​(α,α)=0, the limit may be non-Gaussian or may occur at a slower non-parametric scale. Entropic regularization smooths the dual potentials and typically restores a conventional first-order CLT for fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ, even under weak assumptions on the cost. If the target is unregularized OT, however, this statistical expansion must still be balanced against the bias Lcϵ(α,β)−Lc(α,β)\MK_c^\epsilon(\alpha,\beta)-\MK_c(\alpha,\beta)Lcϵ​(α,β)−Lc​(α,β). Thus Sample Complexity gives dimension-dependent magnitudes, while the present section identifies the local asymptotic constants and covariance formulas needed for inference.

Sketching Sinkhorn in Linear Time¶

The statistical results above explain why entropic OT is attractive at fixed temperature, but they also expose a computational tension. Sampling the marginals replaces the input laws by empirical measures and reduces the problem to finitely many support points; subsampling or coarsening these supports is governed by the sample-complexity estimates of this chapter. Even after the supports are fixed, however, a Sinkhorn sweep still costs O(nm)O(nm)O(nm), because it repeatedly applies the Gibbs kernel to vectors. Kernel sketching attacks this second bottleneck: it keeps the sampled marginals fixed and samples, or otherwise compresses, the feature representation of the kernel used by Sinkhorn. With a rank RRR factorization, NitN_{\rm it}Nit​ scaling sweeps cost O(Nit(n+m)R)O(N_{\rm it}(n+m)R)O(Nit​(n+m)R), which is linear in the support sizes only when both the required rank and the iteration count are controlled. The rank generally depends on dimension, temperature, and target accuracy.

PSD Kernels and Ordinary Feature Sketches¶

The RKHS/MMD section, Dual RKHS Norms and Maximum Mean Discrepancies, already used positive semidefinite kernels to define Hilbertian discrepancies between measures. Recall that a symmetric kernel k:X×X→Rk:\Xx\times\Xx\to\RRk:X×X→R is positive semidefinite if, for every finite family (xi)i=1n(x_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​)i=1n​, the Gram matrix (k(xi,xj))ij(k(x_i,x_j))_{ij}(k(xi​,xj​))ij​ is positive semidefinite. Many scalable kernel methods start from an integral feature representation

k(x,y)=∫Z⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp dξ(z),ϕ:X×Z→Rp,k(x,y)=\int_Z \dotp{\phi(x,z)}{\phi(y,z)}_{\RR^p}\,d\xi(z), \qquad \phi:\Xx\times Z\to\RR^p,k(x,y)=∫Z​⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp​dξ(z),ϕ:X×Z→Rp,
(69)

where ξ\xiξ is a latent distribution. Drawing z1,…,zr∼ξz_1,\ldots,z_r\sim\xiz1​,…,zr​∼ξ gives

k~r(x,y)=1r∑ℓ=1r⟨ϕ(x,zℓ),ϕ(y,zℓ)⟩Rp.\widetilde k_r(x,y) = \frac1r\sum_{\ell=1}^r \dotp{\phi(x,z_\ell)}{\phi(y,z_\ell)}_{\RR^p}.kr​(x,y)=r1​ℓ=1∑r​⟨ϕ(x,zℓ​),ϕ(y,zℓ​)⟩Rp​.
(70)

This is the classical random-feature principle. For data points (xi)i=1n(x_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​)i=1n​, the dense Gram matrix K=(k(xi,xj))ijK=(k(x_i,x_j))_{ij}K=(k(xi​,xj​))ij​ is replaced by K~=ΦΦ⊤\widetilde K=\Phi\Phi^\topK=ΦΦ⊤, where Φ∈Rn×rp\Phi\in\RR^{n\times rp}Φ∈Rn×rp is the sampled feature matrix with entries Φi,(ℓ,q)=r−1/2ϕq(xi,zℓ)\Phi_{i,(\ell,q)}=r^{-1/2}\phi_q(x_i,z_\ell)Φi,(ℓ,q)​=r−1/2ϕq​(xi​,zℓ​), 1≤ℓ≤r1\leq \ell\leq r1≤ℓ≤r, 1≤q≤p1\leq q\leq p1≤q≤p. The number rrr of sampled latent variables is thus a second sample size, distinct from the number of data points. At this stage no positivity of ϕ\phiϕ is assumed; signed or oscillatory features are exactly what make Fourier sketches useful.

For translation-invariant kernels on Rd\RR^dRd, Bochner’s theorem gives the standard Fourier sketch. If k(x,y)=κ(x−y)k(x,y)=\kappa(x-y)k(x,y)=κ(x−y) and κ(t)=∫ei⟨ω,t⟩ dΛ(ω)\kappa(t)=\int e^{i\dotp{\omega}{t}}\,d\Lambda(\omega)κ(t)=∫ei⟨ω,t⟩dΛ(ω), with Λ\LambdaΛ a positive spectral measure, one may use real features ϕ(x,ω)=(cos⁡⟨ω,x⟩,sin⁡⟨ω,x⟩)\phi(x,\omega)=(\cos\dotp{\omega}{x},\sin\dotp{\omega}{x})ϕ(x,ω)=(cos⟨ω,x⟩,sin⟨ω,x⟩). For the Gaussian kernel kσ(x,y)=exp⁡(−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2))k_\sigma(x,y)=\exp(-\norm{x-y}^2/(2\sigma^2))kσ​(x,y)=exp(−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2)), this corresponds to ω∼N(0,σ−2Id)\omega\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^{-2}\Id)ω∼N(0,σ−2Id). This random Fourier feature construction was introduced by Rahimi and Recht to accelerate large-scale kernel machines Rahimi & Recht, 2007; its statistical role for kernel ridge regression and related supervised methods is analyzed, for instance, in Rudi & Rosasco, 2017Avron et al., 2017.

The difficulty is that Sinkhorn is not a generic kernel method: it divides by K~v\widetilde K vKv and, in dual variables, applies logarithms. Thus one needs K~ij>0\widetilde K_{ij}>0Kij​>0, preferably with a relative error on the entries, because −ϵlog⁡Kij-\epsilon\log K_{ij}−ϵlogKij​ is the effective cost. This is a more stringent requirement than the usual spectral or Frobenius approximation of a PSD Gram matrix.

The next proposition is not a substitute for the sharp low-rank Sinkhorn theory. It is an elementary concentration lemma whose role is to isolate the two facts that matter for Sinkhorn: positivity of the approximate kernel and accuracy after taking logarithms. The full algorithmic statements rely on more refined Nyström or Gaussian-kernel approximations together with stability of Sinkhorn scaling Altschuler et al., 2018Altschuler et al., 2019.

This proposition pinpoints the obstruction. When ϵ\epsilonϵ is small or the data diameter is large, κ=min⁡Kij\kappa=\min K_{ij}κ=minKij​ can be exponentially small, so an ordinary signed sketch may need a very large rrr just to keep all entries positive. What Sinkhorn really needs is relative control of the kernel, equivalently additive control of the sketched costs. Positive features do not solve the whole approximation problem, but they remove the most basic failure mode, negative entries in K~\widetilde KK. The log-normal positive features below are unbounded, so this Hoeffding proposition does not apply to them without truncation or a different concentration argument.

Available worst-case bounds retain explicit dimension dependence. For the quadratic cost on points contained in a radius-RRR ball of Rd\RR^dRd, the Nyström analysis of Altschuler, Bach, Rudi and Niles-Weed Altschuler et al., 2019 studies Kij=exp⁡(−η∥xi−xj∥2)K_{ij}=\exp(-\eta\norm{x_i-x_j}^2)Kij​=exp(−η∥xi​−xj​∥2) and bounds the effective rank by a quantity of the form

r∗(X,η,ϵ0)≲(ηR2+log⁡(n/ϵ0))dr_\ast(X,\eta,\epsilon_0) \lesssim \left(\eta R^2+\log(n/\epsilon_0)\right)^dr∗​(X,η,ϵ0​)≲(ηR2+log(n/ϵ0​))d
(82)

up to universal constants and harmless logarithms. Thus the resulting Sinkhorn computation is near-linear in nnn once this rank is fixed, but the required rank is polynomial in the inverse kernel bandwidth, with exponent ddd and only logarithmic dependence on nnn in this bound. When the same machinery is used to approximate unregularized quadratic OT to additive accuracy τ\tauτ, one takes η\etaη of order τ−1log⁡n\tau^{-1}\log nτ−1logn, so the complexity contains a factor τ−O(d)\tau^{-O(d)}τ−O(d), often summarized informally as an ϵ−d\epsilon^{-d}ϵ−d-type dependence on the target precision. The same work also explains why this can be much better on data with lower intrinsic dimension.

Positive Features and Total Positivity¶

A positive feature sketch asks for more than positive semidefiniteness. In finite dimension, let

DNNn={A∈Rn×n:A⪰0, Aij≥0},CPn={BB⊤:B∈R+n×q for some q≥1}.\mathrm{DNN}_n=\{A\in\RR^{n\times n}: A\succeq0,\ A_{ij}\geq0\}, \qquad \mathrm{CP}_n=\{BB^\top: B\in\RR_+^{n\times q}\hbox{ for some }q\geq1\}.DNNn​={A∈Rn×n:A⪰0, Aij​≥0},CPn​={BB⊤:B∈R+n×q​ for some q≥1}.
(83)

Matrices in DNNn\mathrm{DNN}_nDNNn​ are doubly nonnegative, while matrices in CPn\mathrm{CP}_nCPn​ are completely positive. One always has CPn⊂DNNn\mathrm{CP}_n\subset\mathrm{DNN}_nCPn​⊂DNNn​, with equality for n≤4n\leq4n≤4 and strict inclusion for n≥5n\geq5n≥5 Berman & Shaked-Monderer, 2003Burer et al., 2009. Checking membership in the completely positive cone is computationally hard: strong membership is NP-hard, and weak membership for the completely positive cone and its copositive dual is NP-hard Dickinson & Gijben, 2014.

For kernels, it is useful to distinguish the two corresponding notions. A kernel kkk is doubly positive if every finite Gram matrix belongs to DNNn\mathrm{DNN}_nDNNn​, i.e. if kkk is PSD and pointwise nonnegative. It is totally positive in the positive-feature sense if every finite Gram matrix belongs to CPn\mathrm{CP}_nCPn​. This terminology should not be confused with Karlin’s classical total positivity, which concerns nonnegativity of all minors of an ordered kernel Karlin, 1968; it is a complete-positive-type condition, studied for instance in DeCorte et al., 2022.

The positive-feature construction of Scetbon and Cuturi Scetbon & Cuturi, 2020 makes the reason for this definition direct. If

k(x,y)=∫Z⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp dξ(z),ϕ(x,z)∈R+p,k(x,y)=\int_Z\dotp{\phi(x,z)}{\phi(y,z)}_{\RR^p}\,d\xi(z), \qquad \phi(x,z)\in\RR_+^p,k(x,y)=∫Z​⟨ϕ(x,z),ϕ(y,z)⟩Rp​dξ(z),ϕ(x,z)∈R+p​,
(84)

then every finite Gram matrix is a conic combination of rank-one matrices vv⊤vv^\topvv⊤ with v≥0v\geq0v≥0, and hence is completely positive. Conversely, on a fixed finite set, K∈CPnK\in\mathrm{CP}_nK∈CPn​ is exactly the existence of a nonnegative factorization K=BB⊤K=BB^\topK=BB⊤. Thus total positivity is the relevant finite-sample kernel condition behind positive random features. For rectangular source--target matrices, one applies the same statement to the Gram matrix on the union of the sampled source and target points and then extracts its n×mn\times mn×m cross block.

Proposition: Basic Closure of Totally Positive Kernels

Nonnegative sums and pointwise products of totally positive kernels are totally positive. The same holds for measurable nonnegative mixtures whenever the resulting kernel is finite. In particular, positive autocorrelations

k(x,y)=∫g(u−x)g(u−y) du,g≥0,k(x,y)=\int g(u-x)g(u-y)\,du, \qquad g\geq0,k(x,y)=∫g(u−x)g(u−y)du,g≥0,
(85)

and all nonnegative mixtures of such kernels are totally positive.

Proof

For sums, concatenate the nonnegative features and rescale them by the square roots of the nonnegative coefficients. For products, tensor the nonnegative features:

⟨ϕ1(x,z1),ϕ1(y,z1)⟩⟨ϕ2(x,z2),ϕ2(y,z2)⟩=⟨ϕ1(x,z1)⊗ϕ2(x,z2),ϕ1(y,z1)⊗ϕ2(y,z2)⟩.\dotp{\phi_1(x,z_1)}{\phi_1(y,z_1)} \dotp{\phi_2(x,z_2)}{\phi_2(y,z_2)} = \dotp{\phi_1(x,z_1)\otimes\phi_2(x,z_2)} {\phi_1(y,z_1)\otimes\phi_2(y,z_2)}.⟨ϕ1​(x,z1​),ϕ1​(y,z1​)⟩⟨ϕ2​(x,z2​),ϕ2​(y,z2​)⟩=⟨ϕ1​(x,z1​)⊗ϕ2​(x,z2​),ϕ1​(y,z1​)⊗ϕ2​(y,z2​)⟩.
(86)

The tensor feature remains entrywise nonnegative. A measurable mixture is a limit of conic combinations in the closed completely positive cone on every finite point set. The autocorrelation formula is already a positive feature representation with latent variable uuu and scalar feature g(u−x)g(u-x)g(u−x).

The Gaussian Gibbs kernels used by Sinkhorn admit an especially simple positive feature representation, which is the construction exploited by Scetbon and Cuturi Scetbon & Cuturi, 2020. The same construction extends to the generalized Gaussian kernels e−∥x−y∥p/ϵe^{-\norm{x-y}^p/\epsilon}e−∥x−y∥p/ϵ for 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2, because these kernels are mixtures of Gaussian kernels. This is the Schoenberg--Bernstein mechanism behind the positive definiteness of radial stable kernels Schoenberg, 1938Berg et al., 1984.

Let 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2, ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, and

exp⁡(−taϵ)=∫0+∞e−λt dνa,ϵ(λ),t≥0.\exp\left(-\frac{t^a}{\epsilon}\right) = \int_0^{+\infty} e^{-\lambda t}\,d\nu_{a,\epsilon}(\lambda), \qquad t\geq0.exp(−ϵta​)=∫0+∞​e−λtdνa,ϵ​(λ),t≥0.

k~p,ϵ(x,y)=∑ℓ=1rφℓ(x)φℓ(y),φℓ(x)=r−1/2ϕp(x,Λℓ,Zℓ),\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \sum_{\ell=1}^r \varphi_\ell(x)\varphi_\ell(y), \qquad \varphi_\ell(x)=r^{-1/2}\phi_p(x,\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell),kp,ϵ​(x,y)=ℓ=1∑r​φℓ​(x)φℓ​(y),φℓ​(x)=r−1/2ϕp​(x,Λℓ​,Zℓ​),
(93)

is an unbiased nonnegative feature sketch of kp,ϵk_{p,\epsilon}kp,ϵ​.

For p=2p=2p=2, the mixing law reduces to the Dirac mass ν1,ϵ=δ1/ϵ\nu_{1,\epsilon}=\delta_{1/\epsilon}ν1,ϵ​=δ1/ϵ​, which recovers the usual Gaussian feature formula.

Proof

The function s↦e−sas\mapsto e^{-s^a}s↦e−sa is completely monotone for 0<a≤10<a\leq10<a≤1. Bernstein’s theorem therefore gives the Laplace-transform representation of a positive aaa-stable random variable SaS_aSa​. The scaling Λ=ϵ−1/aSa\Lambda=\epsilon^{-1/a}S_aΛ=ϵ−1/aSa​ gives

Ee−tΛ=exp⁡(−taϵ),\mathbb E e^{-t\Lambda} = \exp\left(-\frac{t^a}{\epsilon}\right),Ee−tΛ=exp(−ϵta​),
(94)

which is the displayed representation by νa,ϵ\nu_{a,\epsilon}νa,ϵ​. Applying this identity with t=∥x−y∥2t=\norm{x-y}^2t=∥x−y∥2 gives the Gaussian-mixture formula.

Conditionally on Λ=λ\Lambda=\lambdaΛ=λ, the Gaussian moment-generating function gives

EZ(ϕp(x,λ,Z)ϕp(y,λ,Z))=exp⁡(−∥qx(λ)∥2−∥qy(λ)∥2)EZ(exp⁡⟨Z,qx(λ)+qy(λ)⟩)=exp⁡(−12∥qx(λ)−qy(λ)∥2)=exp⁡(−λ∥x−y∥2).\begin{aligned} \mathbb E_Z\left(\phi_p(x,\lambda,Z)\phi_p(y,\lambda,Z)\right) &= \exp\left(-\norm{q_x(\lambda)}^2-\norm{q_y(\lambda)}^2\right) \mathbb E_Z\left(\exp\dotp{Z}{q_x(\lambda)+q_y(\lambda)}\right) \\ &= \exp\left(-\frac12\norm{q_x(\lambda)-q_y(\lambda)}^2\right) = \exp\left(-\lambda\norm{x-y}^2\right). \end{aligned}EZ​(ϕp​(x,λ,Z)ϕp​(y,λ,Z))​=exp(−∥qx​(λ)∥2−∥qy​(λ)∥2)EZ​(exp⟨Z,qx​(λ)+qy​(λ)⟩)=exp(−21​∥qx​(λ)−qy​(λ)∥2)=exp(−λ∥x−y∥2).​
(95)

Taking the expectation over Λ\LambdaΛ gives kp,ϵk_{p,\epsilon}kp,ϵ​. Since ϕp\phi_pϕp​ is positive, this is a positive-feature representation; hence every finite Gram matrix is completely positive. The Monte-Carlo sketch is just the empirical average of this representation.

Remark: The range 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2

The restriction 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2 is essential. Schoenberg’s theorem says that x↦e−γ∥x∥px\mapsto e^{-\gamma\norm{x}^p}x↦e−γ∥x∥p is positive definite on every Euclidean space precisely in this range. For p>2p>2p>2, some finite Gram matrices have a negative eigenvalue, so no universal positive-feature factorization should be expected.

For p<2p<2p<2, the positive stable mixing variable is heavy tailed. For x≠x0x\neq x_0x=x0​,

EZϕp(x,Λ,Z)4=exp⁡(8Λ∥x−x0∥2),\mathbb E_Z\phi_p(x,\Lambda,Z)^4 =\exp\left(8\Lambda\norm{x-x_0}^2\right),EZ​ϕp​(x,Λ,Z)4=exp(8Λ∥x−x0​∥2),
(96)

whose expectation over Λ\LambdaΛ is infinite. Unbiasedness therefore does not give a finite-variance Monte-Carlo sketch; practical implementations need truncation, quadrature, variance reduction, or another positive representation. The p=2p=2p=2 case avoids this issue because Λ=1/ϵ\Lambda=1/\epsilonΛ=1/ϵ is deterministic.

Choosing x0x_0x0​ near the data can reduce the dynamic range of the features without changing the kernel. More generally, Gaussian scale mixtures give many radial totally positive kernels, including standard covariance families used in Gaussian processes Rasmussen & Williams, 2006.

The gap between doubly positive and totally positive kernels is real. On the circle, consider

kλ(x,y)=λ+cos⁡2(x−y2),λ>0.k_\lambda(x,y)=\lambda+\cos^2\left(\frac{x-y}{2}\right), \qquad \lambda>0.kλ​(x,y)=λ+cos2(2x−y​),λ>0.
(97)

This kernel is PSD and strictly positive pointwise, since cos⁡2(t/2)=(1+cos⁡t)/2\cos^2(t/2)=(1+\cos t)/2cos2(t/2)=(1+cost)/2 has nonnegative Fourier coefficients and λ\lambdaλ adds a positive constant mode. For λ=1/20\lambda=1/20λ=1/20, however, its Gram matrix on five equally spaced points is not completely positive. The Horn copositive matrix HHH satisfies ⟨H,B⟩≥0\langle H,B\rangle\geq0⟨H,B⟩≥0 for every completely positive matrix BBB, but the five-point Gram matrix KKK gives

⟨H,K⟩=214−552<0.\langle H,K\rangle = \frac{21}{4}-\frac{5\sqrt5}{2}<0.⟨H,K⟩=421​−255​​<0.
(98)

Thus K∈DNN5∖CP5K\in\mathrm{DNN}_5\setminus\mathrm{CP}_5K∈DNN5​∖CP5​, and the kernel is doubly positive but not totally positive.

Positive Sketches for Sinkhorn¶

For the ppp-power cost cp(x,y)=∥x−y∥pc_p(x,y)=\norm{x-y}^pcp​(x,y)=∥x−y∥p, with 0<p≤20<p\leq20<p≤2, the Sinkhorn Gibbs kernel is the generalized Gaussian kernel

kp,ϵ(x,y)=exp⁡(−∥x−y∥pϵ).k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \exp\left(-\frac{\norm{x-y}^p}{\epsilon}\right).kp,ϵ​(x,y)=exp(−ϵ∥x−y∥p​).
(99)

The factor 1/p1/p1/p, often used in the definition of WppW_p^pWpp​, only rescales ϵ\epsilonϵ. For p≥1p\geq1p≥1, this is the usual ppp-Wasserstein power cost; for 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, it should be read simply as a concave power transport cost. Proposition Proposition: Generalized Gaussian Positive Features gives a positive factorization of this kernel. With rrr draws (Λℓ,Zℓ)∼νp/2,ϵ⊗N(0,Idd)(\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell)\sim\nu_{p/2,\epsilon}\otimes\mathcal N(0,\Id_d)(Λℓ​,Zℓ​)∼νp/2,ϵ​⊗N(0,Idd​), define the normalized features

φℓ(x)=r−1/2ϕp(x,Λℓ,Zℓ),1≤ℓ≤r.\varphi_\ell(x)=r^{-1/2}\phi_p(x,\Lambda_\ell,Z_\ell), \qquad 1\leq \ell\leq r .φℓ​(x)=r−1/2ϕp​(x,Λℓ​,Zℓ​),1≤ℓ≤r.
(100)

They satisfy

k~p,ϵ(x,y)=∑ℓ=1rφℓ(x)φℓ(y)≥0,E[k~p,ϵ(x,y)]=kp,ϵ(x,y).\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y) = \sum_{\ell=1}^r\varphi_\ell(x)\varphi_\ell(y) \geq0, \qquad \mathbb E[\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y)]=k_{p,\epsilon}(x,y).kp,ϵ​(x,y)=ℓ=1∑r​φℓ​(x)φℓ​(y)≥0,E[kp,ϵ​(x,y)]=kp,ϵ​(x,y).
(101)

The corresponding matrices (ΦX)iℓ=φℓ(xi)(\Phi_X)_{i\ell}=\varphi_\ell(x_i)(ΦX​)iℓ​=φℓ​(xi​) and (ΦY)jℓ=φℓ(yj)(\Phi_Y)_{j\ell}=\varphi_\ell(y_j)(ΦY​)jℓ​=φℓ​(yj​) give a positive factorization K~=ΦXΦY⊤\widetilde K=\Phi_X\Phi_Y^\topK=ΦX​ΦY⊤​. Sinkhorn can therefore be run safely on the sketched kernel, and the resulting plan is represented as

P~=diag⁡(u)ΦXΦY⊤diag⁡(v)=LR⊤,L=diag⁡(u)ΦX,R=diag⁡(v)ΦY.\widetilde P = \diag(u)\Phi_X\Phi_Y^\top\diag(v) = LR^\top, \qquad L=\diag(u)\Phi_X, \quad R=\diag(v)\Phi_Y .P=diag(u)ΦX​ΦY⊤​diag(v)=LR⊤,L=diag(u)ΦX​,R=diag(v)ΦY​.
(102)

The output is the exact entropic coupling for the sketched effective cost c~p,ϵ=−ϵlog⁡k~p,ϵ\widetilde c_{p,\epsilon}=-\epsilon\log\widetilde k_{p,\epsilon}cp,ϵ​=−ϵlogkp,ϵ​, and it approximates the original WpW_pWp​-type entropic problem only insofar as this logarithmic kernel approximation is accurate. This route is complementary to worst-case near-linear Sinkhorn analyses Altschuler et al., 2017, low-rank Gaussian-kernel approximations for quadratic transport Altschuler et al., 2018, and factored-coupling models in which the coupling itself is constrained to have low rank Scetbon et al., 2021.

The top row shows the entropic couplings, while the bottom row shows the matching effective costs c~ϵ(x,y)=−ϵlog⁡k~ϵ(x,y)\widetilde c_\epsilon(x,y)=-\epsilon\log\widetilde k_\epsilon(x,y)cϵ​(x,y)=−ϵlogkϵ​(x,y) with black level sets. The dense Gaussian Gibbs kernel gives the usual entropic plan and the quadratic cost ∣x−y∣2|x-y|^2∣x−y∣2. A sufficiently rich rank-40 positive-feature sketch remains visually close to both, whereas rank-10 and rank-3 sketches still enforce the prescribed marginals after Sinkhorn scaling but progressively lose the geometric concentration of the true coupling because the logarithmic kernel approximation has become too coarse.

Connection with Linear Attention¶

The same algebra appears in transformer attention, studied later from a continuous-depth transport viewpoint in Evolution in Depth of Transformers. A softmax attention matrix has entries proportional to exp⁡(⟨qi,kj⟩)\exp(\dotp{q_i}{k_j})exp(⟨qi​,kj​⟩); linear-attention methods replace this positive kernel by features Φ(qi)⊤Φ(kj)\Phi(q_i)^\top\Phi(k_j)Φ(qi​)⊤Φ(kj​), so that attention can be applied as Φ(Q)(Φ(K)⊤V)\Phi(Q)(\Phi(K)^\top V)Φ(Q)(Φ(K)⊤V) rather than by forming the full n×nn\times nn×n matrix Katharopoulos et al., 2020Choromanski et al., 2021Wang et al., 2020Xiong et al., 2021. Sinkhorn sketching is the transport analogue of this idea: replace the Gibbs matrix by a positive feature factorization, keep only the scaling vectors and feature factors, and control the approximation in the logarithmic scale relevant to entropic potentials. The transport case is more constrained, however, since the approximate kernel is reused inside nonlinear normalizations until the prescribed marginals are reached for the sketched problem.
